search.placeholder: Type a place, a nation, or a prime minister
welcome: Come and see the places, nations, and leaders of Canada.
home.fact: Ottawa is the capital of Canada. It is in Ontario.
ottawa.title: Ottawa
ottawa.body: Ottawa is the capital of Canada. Ottawa is in Ontario. It is not a province.
part.province: {name} is a province. It is part of Canada.
part.territory: {name} is a territory. It is part of Canada.
nations.notOne: First Nations, Inuit, and Métis are not one people.
nations.hundreds: There are hundreds of First Nations. This site can show only some.
nations.schools: Many children were sent away to schools that tried to stop their languages.
nations.mapNote: These marks show homelands. They are not old borders.
nations.today: Many descendants live in these homelands now.
time.bridge: Now meet the prime ministers in the order they served. The first one began in 1867.
quiz.maxTeams: You can have up to 10 teams.
quiz.maxKids: A team can have up to 4 children.
quiz.sameChild: A child may be on more than one team.
quiz.needTeam: Add a team and at least one child.
quiz.question: Question {n} of {total}
install.title: Add to iPhone or iPad
install.body: Use Safari. Tap Share. Then tap Add to Home Screen.
about.3: English and French are the official languages of the country.
about.6: Indigenous nations were here before the provinces.
about.7: A prime minister serves a term.
notFound.title: Try another name.
place.alberta.weather: The Rocky Mountains rise in the west. Prairie and forest cover much of the rest.
place.alberta.symbol: The wild rose is a symbol of Alberta.
place.alberta.peoples: Niitsitapi, Cree, Dene, Métis, Nakoda, and Tsuut'ina have homelands here. Many Indigenous people live here now.
place.alberta.famous: Banff is a famous place you can picture, with mountains and lakes.
place.british-columbia.weather: The coast is often rainy. High mountains stand inland.
place.british-columbia.symbol: The Pacific dogwood is a symbol of British Columbia.
place.british-columbia.peoples: Haida, Kwakwaka'wakw, Nisga'a, and Coast Salish nations have homelands here, and so do many other First Nations. Many Indigenous people live here now.
place.british-columbia.famous: Stanley Park is a famous green place by the sea in Vancouver.
place.manitoba.weather: The south is flat prairie. The north has lakes and forest.
place.manitoba.symbol: The prairie crocus is a symbol of Manitoba.
place.manitoba.peoples: Cree, Anishinaabe, Dakota, Dene, and Métis have homelands here. Many Indigenous people live here now.
place.manitoba.famous: Churchill is a famous place where people picture polar bears on the snow.
place.new-brunswick.weather: Forest covers much of the land. Winters bring snow.
place.new-brunswick.symbol: The purple violet is a symbol of New Brunswick.
place.new-brunswick.peoples: Wolastoqiyik, Mi'kmaq, and Peskotomuhkati have homelands here. Many Indigenous people live here now.
place.new-brunswick.famous: The Bay of Fundy is famous for very high tides.
place.newfoundland-and-labrador.weather: Rocky coasts and fog are common. Labrador has forest and tundra.
place.newfoundland-and-labrador.symbol: The pitcher plant is a symbol of Newfoundland and Labrador.
place.newfoundland-and-labrador.peoples: Innu, Inuit, and Mi'kmaq have homelands here. Many Indigenous people live here now.
place.newfoundland-and-labrador.famous: Signal Hill looks over the harbour at St. John's.
place.nova-scotia.weather: The sea is close by. Fog can roll in.
place.nova-scotia.symbol: The mayflower is a symbol of Nova Scotia.
place.nova-scotia.peoples: The Mi'kmaq have homelands here. Many Indigenous people live here now.
place.nova-scotia.famous: Peggy's Cove has a lighthouse on the rocks.
place.ontario.weather: The Great Lakes are huge. The north has forest and lakes.
place.ontario.symbol: The white trillium is a symbol of Ontario.
place.ontario.peoples: Anishinaabe, Haudenosaunee, and Cree have homelands here, and so do other nations. Many Indigenous people live here now.
place.ontario.famous: Niagara Falls is a huge waterfall you can picture.
place.prince-edward-island.weather: The island is low and green. The wind can be strong.
place.prince-edward-island.symbol: The pink lady's slipper is a symbol of Prince Edward Island.
place.prince-edward-island.peoples: The Mi'kmaq have homelands here. They call the island Epekwitk. Many Indigenous people live here now.
place.prince-edward-island.famous: Cavendish has green fields and red cliffs by the sea.
place.quebec.weather: The St. Lawrence River runs through the south. The north is vast forest and tundra.
place.quebec.symbol: The snowy owl is a symbol of Quebec.
place.quebec.peoples: Innu, Wendat, Anishinaabe, Cree, and Kanien'kehá:ka have homelands here, and so do other nations. Many Indigenous people live here now.
place.quebec.famous: The old stone walls of Quebec City are easy to picture.
place.saskatchewan.weather: The south is flat prairie. The north is forest.
place.saskatchewan.symbol: The western red lily is a symbol of Saskatchewan.
place.saskatchewan.peoples: Cree, Anishinaabe, Nakoda, Dakota, Dene, and Métis have homelands here. Many Indigenous people live here now.
place.saskatchewan.famous: Cypress Hills rise above the prairie.
place.northwest-territories.weather: Great lakes, forest, and tundra fill the land. Winters are long and cold.
place.northwest-territories.symbol: Mountain avens is a symbol of the Northwest Territories.
place.northwest-territories.peoples: Dene, Inuvialuit, and Métis have homelands here. Many Indigenous people live here now.
place.northwest-territories.famous: Great Slave Lake is a huge lake you can picture from the shore.
place.nunavut.weather: The land is Arctic tundra. Winters are long and very cold.
place.nunavut.symbol: Purple saxifrage is a symbol of Nunavut.
place.nunavut.peoples: Inuit have homelands here. Many Inuit live here now.
place.nunavut.famous: Iqaluit sits by the sea, and stone inuksuit stand on the land.
place.yukon.weather: Mountains and valleys fill the territory. Winters are cold.
place.yukon.symbol: Fireweed is a symbol of Yukon.
place.yukon.peoples: First Nations including Tlingit, Gwich'in, and Kaska have homelands here, and so do others. Many Indigenous people live here now.
nation.haudenosaunee.englishLine: In English many people say the Six Nations.
nation.haudenosaunee.home: Haudenosaunee homelands include parts of southern Ontario and Quebec, and land across the river in what is now the United States.
nation.haudenosaunee.fact: The Haudenosaunee are a league of nations. They include the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca, and Tuscarora.
nation.haudenosaunee.now: Many Haudenosaunee people live in these homelands now.
nation.haudenosaunee.person: Tom Longboat was a Haudenosaunee runner.
nation.anishinaabe.englishLine: In English you may also hear Ojibwe for one Anishinaabe people.
nation.anishinaabe.home: Anishinaabe homelands are around the Great Lakes and reach into the prairies.
nation.anishinaabe.fact: Wild rice, called manoomin, is an important food for many Anishinaabe.
nation.anishinaabe.now: Many Anishinaabe people live in these homelands now.
nation.cree.englishLine: Cree is the common English name. Peoples in this family also use names such as nêhiyawak and Eeyou.
nation.cree.home: Cree homelands stretch across a wide part of Canada, from Quebec to Alberta.
nation.cree.fact: Cree languages are spoken across that wide land.
nation.cree.now: Many Cree people live in these homelands now.
nation.mikmaq.englishLine: Mi'kmaq is the common English name. L'nu is also used.
nation.mikmaq.home: Mi'kmaq homelands are in the Atlantic region, including Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and parts of Quebec and Newfoundland.
nation.mikmaq.fact: Prince Edward Island is called Epekwitk in Mi'kmaq.
nation.mikmaq.now: Many Mi'kmaq people live in these homelands now.
nation.mikmaq.person: Rita Joe was a Mi'kmaq poet.
nation.siksika.englishLine: Siksika means Blackfoot. Siksika is one of the Niitsitapi nations.
nation.siksika.home: Siksika homelands are in southern Alberta.
nation.siksika.fact: The Niitsitapi include Siksika, Kainai, and Piikani.
nation.siksika.now: Many Siksika people live in these homelands now.
nation.haida.englishLine: Haida is the common English name.
nation.haida.home: Haida homelands include Haida Gwaii, islands off the north coast of British Columbia.
nation.haida.fact: Many Haida artists carve cedar poles and canoes.
nation.haida.now: Many Haida people live in these homelands now.
nation.haida.person: Bill Reid was a Haida artist.
nation.dene.englishLine: Dene is the common English name.
nation.dene.home: Dene homelands include much of the Northwest Territories and parts of the northern provinces.
nation.dene.fact: Dene means "the people" in their language.
nation.dene.now: Many Dene people live in these homelands now.
nation.inuit.englishLine: Inuit is the common English name. One person is an Inuk.
nation.inuit.home: Inuit homelands are in the Arctic, including Nunavut, northern Quebec, northern Labrador, and parts of the Northwest Territories.
nation.inuit.now: Many Inuit live in these homelands now.
nation.inuit.person: Kenojuak Ashevak was an Inuit artist.
nation.metis.englishLine: Métis is the common English name.
nation.metis.home: Métis homelands include the prairies, and Métis people live in many other parts of Canada too.
nation.metis.fact: The Métis are a distinct Indigenous people. They are not First Nations, and they are not Inuit.
nation.metis.now: Many Métis people live in these homelands now.
nation.kwakwakawakw.englishLine: Kwakwaka'wakw is the common English name.
nation.kwakwakawakw.home: Kwakwaka'wakw homelands are on northern Vancouver Island and the nearby mainland in British Columbia.
nation.kwakwakawakw.fact: Kwakwaka'wakw artists are known for cedar houses and carved art.
nation.kwakwakawakw.now: Many Kwakwaka'wakw people live in these homelands now.
nation.nisgaa.englishLine: Nisga'a is the common English name.
nation.nisgaa.home: Nisga'a homelands are in the Nass Valley in northern British Columbia.
nation.nisgaa.fact: The Nass River runs through Nisga'a homelands.
nation.nisgaa.now: Many Nisga'a people live in these homelands now.
nation.innu.englishLine: Innu is the common English name.
nation.innu.home: Innu homelands are in Quebec and Labrador. They call this land Nitassinan.
nation.innu.fact: Nitassinan means the land of the Innu.
nation.innu.now: Many Innu people live in these homelands now.
leader.john-a-macdonald.f1: He was the first prime minister.
leader.alexander-mackenzie.f1: He was a stonemason before he led the country.
leader.alexander-mackenzie.f2: He was the second prime minister.
leader.john-abbott.f1: He was prime minister for a short time.
leader.john-abbott.f2: He had also been a mayor of Montreal.
leader.mackenzie-bowell.f1: He worked as a newspaper printer before politics.
leader.charles-tupper.f1: He was prime minister for a few months in 1896.
leader.wilfrid-laurier.f1: He was the first French-speaking prime minister.
leader.robert-borden.f2: He was prime minister for nearly nine years.
leader.william-lyon-mackenzie-king.f1: He was prime minister three times.
leader.william-lyon-mackenzie-king.f2: He served longer than any other prime minister.
leader.rb-bennett.f1: He was born in New Brunswick.
leader.rb-bennett.f2: He was prime minister during hard times in the 1930s.
leader.louis-st-laurent.f2: He was a lawyer from Quebec.
leader.john-diefenbaker.f2: He had thick wavy white hair.
leader.lester-b-pearson.f1: He won the Nobel Peace Prize.
leader.lester-b-pearson.f2: He liked to wear a bow tie.
leader.pierre-trudeau.f2: He wore a rose on his jacket.
leader.joe-clark.f1: He became prime minister at age 39.
leader.john-turner.f1: He was prime minister for a few months in 1984.
leader.brian-mulroney.f2: He served for nearly nine years.
leader.kim-campbell.f1: She was the first woman to be prime minister.
leader.stephen-harper.f1: He was born in Ontario and later lived in Alberta.
leader.stephen-harper.f2: He served for nearly ten years.
leader.justin-trudeau.f1: He is the son of Pierre Trudeau.
leader.mark-carney.f1: He led the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England.
leader.mark-carney.f2: He was born in Fort Smith, in the Northwest Territories.
time.nations.title: Indigenous nations
time.nations.body: First Nations, Inuit, and Métis were here long before the provinces. They are not one people.
time.1867.body: Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia join Canada. John A. Macdonald becomes the first prime minister.
time.1870.body: Manitoba and the Northwest Territories become part of Canada.
time.1871.body: British Columbia joins Canada. The capital is Victoria.
time.1873.body: Prince Edward Island joins Canada. The capital is Charlottetown.
time.1898.body: Yukon becomes a territory. The capital is Whitehorse.
time.1949.body: Newfoundland and Labrador joins Canada. It is one province.
time.1999.body: Nunavut becomes a territory. The capital is Iqaluit. Inuit homelands are here.
q.year: In what year did {place} join Canada?
q.symbol: Which sentence is true about a symbol of {place}?
q.water: Which place is across the water from {place}?
w.kind.province: {place} is a province. It is part of Canada.
w.kind.territory: {place} is a territory. It is part of Canada.
q.first: In what year did {name} first become prime minister?
q.today: Which sentence is true about {name} today?
c.today: Many descendants live in the homelands now.
w.today: Many {name} descendants live in the homelands now.
q.reverse: {capital} is the capital of which place?
g.provinces: How many provinces does Canada have?
g.territories: How many territories does Canada have?
g.together: How many provinces and territories are there together?
g.together.why: Ten provinces and three territories make 13.
g.capital: What is the capital of Canada?
g.capital.why: Ottawa is the capital of Canada.
g.ottawaNot.a: Ottawa is the capital of Canada. It is not a province.
g.ottawaNot.why: Ottawa is the capital of Canada. It is in Ontario. It is not a province.
g.langs: What are the official languages of Canada?
g.langs.why: English and French are the official languages of the country.
g.quebec: What is the official language of Quebec?
g.first: Who was the first prime minister?
g.first.why: John A. Macdonald was the first prime minister.
g.woman: Who was the first woman to be prime minister?
g.woman.why: Kim Campbell was the first woman to be prime minister.
g.nl: In what year did Newfoundland and Labrador join Canada?
g.nl.why: Newfoundland and Labrador joined Canada in 1949.
g.now.why: Mark Carney is prime minister now. He is still in office.
g.notOne: First Nations, Inuit, and Métis are…
g.notOne.why: First Nations, Inuit, and Métis are not one people.
g.hundreds: How many First Nations are there?
g.hundreds.why: There are hundreds of First Nations. This site can show only some.
g.term.why: A prime minister serves a term.
g.died1891: Who died while in office in 1891?
g.died1891.why: John A. Macdonald died while in office on 6 June 1891.
g.died1894: Who died while in office in 1894?
g.died1894.why: John Thompson died while in office on 12 December 1894.
g.king: How many times did William Lyon Mackenzie King become prime minister?
g.king.why: William Lyon Mackenzie King was prime minister three times.
g.before.a: Indigenous nations were here before the provinces.
g.before.why: Indigenous nations were here before the provinces.
g.campbellFrom: Kim Campbell came from which province?
g.campbellFrom.why: Kim Campbell came from British Columbia.
g.carneyBorn: Mark Carney was born in which territory?
g.carneyBorn.why: Mark Carney was born in Fort Smith, in the Northwest Territories.
g.father: Pierre Trudeau is the father of which later prime minister?
g.father.why: Justin Trudeau is the son of Pierre Trudeau.
g.bow: Which prime minister liked to wear a bow tie?
g.bow.why: Lester B. Pearson liked to wear a bow tie.
g.rose: Which prime minister wore a rose on his jacket?
g.rose.why: Pierre Trudeau wore a rose on his jacket.
p01.title: Colour a maple leaf
p01.s1: Draw a simple leaf with five fat parts.
p01.s3: Leave the paper around it white.
p01.done: The leaf is red and the paper is white.
p02.title: Find a capital together
p02.need: A friend and the Places pages
p03.title: Count the provinces
p04.title: Point to Ottawa
p04.need: The Canada map and a friend
p04.s2: Say that Ottawa is in Ontario.
p04.s3: Ask your friend to say it back.
p04.done: Your friend can say Ottawa is the capital.
p05.title: A red and white card
p05.s2: Colour one side red and leave one side white.
p05.done: The card is red and white.
p06.title: Three place names
p06.need: Paper, a pencil, and a partner
p06.s1: Each child copies two place names.
p06.s3: Star the one you both like to say.
p06.done: Four names are on the paper.
p07.title: Colour a province outline
p07.done: The name is on the shape.
p08.title: Match a year
p08.need: Two children and slips of paper
p08.s3: Match them, then try two more places.
p08.done: Each year sits with the right place.
p09.title: Draw the weather
p09.done: A grown-up can tell the weather in your picture.
p10.title: Five capitals
p10.s2: Write each capital beside the name.
p11.title: Capital quiz
p11.s1: One child asks for a capital.
p11.done: You have asked about five places.
p12.title: North and south
p12.s3: Write which one is farther north.
p12.done: You wrote that Yukon is farther north.
p13.title: Name a neighbour
p13.need: A team and the Manitoba page
p13.s3: Point to those places on the map.
p13.done: The team named two neighbours of Manitoba.
p14.title: A symbol card
p14.done: The card says Alberta and shows a rose.
p15.title: Read a peoples sentence
p15.need: A team and one place page
p15.s2: Read the Indigenous peoples sentence aloud.
p15.s3: Say that many Indigenous people live there now.
p16.title: Ten and three
p16.done: Your paper shows 10 provinces and 3 territories.
p17.title: Find Nunavut
p17.done: The team can point to Nunavut.
p18.title: One province, two names
p18.s3: Write that it is one province.
p18.done: Your paper says it is one province.
p19.title: Four facts
p19.s3: Write each fact in a short line of your own.
p20.title: Two outlines
p20.s1: Each child colours a different province.
p20.s3: Say one way the places differ.
p20.done: Two shapes and two capitals are done.
p21.title: Years in order
p21.s2: Put them in order from earliest to latest.
p21.s3: Add one place name to each year.
p22.title: Beside Saskatchewan
p23.title: Three territories
p23.s1: Write Yukon, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut.
p23.done: Three capitals are on the page.
p24.title: Teach a place
p24.s2: They say the capital, the year, and one fact.
p24.done: The team can say the capital.
p25.title: Official languages
p25.s3: Write that they are the official languages of Canada.
p26.title: Quebec and New Brunswick
p26.s1: One child says Quebec's official language.
p26.s2: The other says New Brunswick is officially bilingual.
p27.title: Ottawa is not a province
p27.s1: Write that Ottawa is the capital.
p27.s2: Write that Ottawa is in Ontario.
p27.s3: Write that Ottawa is not a province.
p27.done: All three sentences are on the paper.
p28.title: Compare two provinces
p28.s2: Write the capital, the year, and one landform for each.
p29.title: A difference
p29.s3: The team says one way they differ.
p29.done: The team agreed on one difference.
p30.title: Five prime ministers
p30.s1: Write Macdonald, Laurier, Pearson, Campbell, and Carney.
p30.s2: Find the year each one first served.
p30.s3: Put the names in that order.
p30.done: The five names are in order.
p31.title: Order a team list
p31.need: A team and slips of paper
p31.s1: Each child writes one prime minister.
p31.s2: Add more names until you have five.
p31.s3: Put them in the order they first served.
p32.title: Not the same
p32.s1: Write: First Nations are not Inuit.
p32.s3: Write: Métis are not First Nations.
p32.done: Three sentences say they are not the same.
p33.title: A plain poster
p33.need: A team and a large sheet
p33.s1: Write that First Nations, Inuit, and Métis are not one people.
p33.s2: Add that there are hundreds of First Nations.
p33.s3: Do not draw anyone in regalia.
p33.done: The poster has those two sentences.
p34.title: Nunavut in two lines
p34.s1: Write that Nunavut became a territory in 1999.
p34.s2: Write that the capital is Iqaluit.
p34.s3: Write that it is part of Canada.
p35.title: Atlantic list
p35.s1: List New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland and Labrador.
p36.title: Explain a symbol
p36.s3: Write which place it belongs to.
p36.done: The symbol and the place are both named.
p37.title: A time strip
p37.s2: Add one place to each date.
p37.s3: Read the strip from left to right.
p38.title: Build the strip
p38.need: A team and a long strip
p38.done: The team read the strip in order.
p39.title: One nation page
p39.s1: Write the name the people use.
p39.s3: Write that descendants live there now.
p39.done: Those three parts are on your page.
p40.title: Two nations
p40.s1: Two children each open a nation page.
p40.s3: Do not say one people matters more.
p40.done: The team heard two true things.
p41.title: A date, not a story
p41.need: The page for John A. Macdonald
p41.s2: Write that he died while in office.
p41.done: The date is written and nothing else was added.
p42.title: Still in office
p42.need: A team and the Leaders pages
p42.s1: Find who is still in office.
p42.done: The team wrote Mark Carney and 2025.
p43.title: Four jumps
p43.s2: Jump to a neighbour, then to another.
p43.s3: Write four place names in a chain.
p43.done: Each place in the chain touches the one before it.
p44.title: Label five places
p44.need: A printed map and a team
p44.s2: Each child labels at least one place.
p45.title: Two language facts
p45.s2: Write that New Brunswick is officially bilingual.
p45.done: Both facts are in your words.
p46.title: A leader card
p46.s2: Write born, and died or still living.
p46.done: Born, died or still living, and the terms are all there.
p47.title: Swap and check
p47.need: A team and two leader pages
p47.s1: Two children each make a leader card.
p47.s3: Check the years on the site.
p48.title: Short terms
p48.s2: Find Kim Campbell or John Turner.
p48.s3: Write the years of those short terms.
p48.done: Two short terms are written with years.
p49.title: Three peoples
p49.s2: Say that First Nations, Inuit, and Métis are not one people.
p49.s3: Say that there are hundreds of First Nations.
p49.done: The team said the talk without ranking anyone.
p50.title: Wide homelands
p50.s2: Write two provinces or territories named on the page.
p50.s3: Write that many descendants live there now.
p50.done: Two places and the now sentence are written.
p51.title: Not old borders
p51.need: A team and the Nations map
p51.s1: Read the sentence under the map.
p51.s2: Each child says it in their own words.
p51.s3: Agree that the marks are not old borders.
p51.done: The team said the marks are not old borders.
p52.title: First and latest
p52.s1: Write the first prime minister and his first year.
p52.s2: Write the latest prime minister and his start year.
p52.s3: Add three names from in between, in order.
p52.done: Five leaders are in time order.
p53.title: Write five questions
p53.s1: Each child writes one question from the site.
p53.s2: Add answers until you have five.
p53.s3: Make sure each question has one right answer.
p53.done: Five questions have answers you can check on the site.
p54.title: One calm fact
p54.s3: Add nothing mean and no rumour.
p55.title: Compare two terms
p55.s1: Open Wilfrid Laurier and Stephen Harper.
p55.s2: Write the years each one served.
p55.s3: Say who served more years, and show the years.
p55.done: You used the years, not a guess about who is better.
p56.title: Check the maths
p56.need: A team and two leader pages
p56.s2: Work out how many years each term lasted.
p56.done: The team agrees on both lengths.
p57.title: Nunavut and Inuit homelands
p57.need: Paper and the Nunavut and Inuit pages
p57.s1: Write that Nunavut is part of Canada.
p57.s2: Write that Inuit homelands are there.
p57.s3: Write that many Inuit live there now.
p58.title: A two-minute talk
p58.s2: Say that nations were here before the provinces.
p58.s3: Do not act out a fight.
p58.done: The talk is calm and under two minutes.
p59.title: Label, then explain
p59.s2: Write where the Atlantic provinces sit.
p59.s3: Write where the three territories sit.
p59.done: The map is labelled and both sentences are written.
p60.title: Host a Quick 10
p60.need: A team and the Quiz page
p60.s2: Play as a team against another team, or take turns.
